story: On August 31st, 2026 the FCC published two separate Universal Service Fund notices on the same day with the same comment deadline, one asking nine times whether AI should administer the fund and one naming Alaska as the example of health care providers who almost never use the FCC's preferred rate methods

claims.claim: The FCC notice titled Maximizing Efficiencies in Universal Service Administration was published in the Federal Register on August 31st, 2026 at volume 91 pages 55826 to 55835.
claims.verbatim: Federal Register, Volume 91, Issue 167, Pages 55826-55835
claims.notes: Page span confirmed on two independent fetches of the govinfo HTML.

claims.claim: The Maximizing Efficiencies in Universal Service Administration notice carries WC Docket No. 26-173 and FCC number 26-52.
claims.verbatim: WC Docket No. 26-173; FCC No. 26-52

claims.claim: The FCC adopted the Maximizing Efficiencies in Universal Service Administration notice on August 6th, 2026 and released it on August 7th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: adopted August 6, 2026; released August 7, 2026

claims.claim: The FCC notice titled Promoting Telehealth in Rural America was published in the Federal Register on August 31st, 2026 at volume 91 pages 55816 to 55825.
claims.verbatim: Volume 91, Issue 167, pages 55816-55825
claims.notes: Same Federal Register issue number, 167, as the AI notice, which confirms same day publication.

claims.claim: The Promoting Telehealth in Rural America notice carries WC Docket No. 17-310 and FCC number 26-54.
claims.verbatim: WC Docket No. 17-310; FCC No. 26-54
claims.notes: Different docket and different FCC number from C02, which establishes these are two separate proceedings.

claims.claim: The FCC adopted the Promoting Telehealth in Rural America notice on August 6th, 2026 and released it on August 7th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: adopted August 6, 2026; released August 7, 2026

claims.claim: Comments on the FCC's universal service administration notice are due on or before September 30th, 2026 and reply comments are due on or before October 30th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: Comments are due on or before September 30, 2026 and reply comments are due on or before October 30, 2026.

claims.claim: Comments on the FCC's rural telehealth notice are due on or before September 30th, 2026 and reply comments are due on or before October 30th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: Comments are due on or before September 30, 2026 and reply comments are due on or before October 30, 2026.
claims.notes: Deadlines are identical to C07. The two proceedings are separate but their comment windows open and close on the same days.

claims.claim: The FCC states that in Alaska in funding year 2024 only 32 of 317 approved Telecom Program requests relied on Methods 1 or 2.
claims.verbatim: in Alaska, in funding year 2024, only 32 of 317 approved Telecom Program requests relied on Methods 1 or 2
claims.notes: Verbatim string reproduced identically on three separate fetches of the page.

claims.claim: The FCC states that in Alaska in funding year 2025 only 34 of 340 approved Telecom Program requests relied on Methods 1 or 2.
claims.verbatim: in funding year 2025, only 34 of 340 approved Telecom Program requests in Alaska relied on Methods 1 or 2
claims.notes: Verbatim string reproduced identically on three separate fetches of the page.

claims.claim: Subtracting the FCC's own figures, 306 of Alaska's 340 approved Telecom Program requests in funding year 2025 did not rely on Methods 1 or 2, which is 90.0 percent.
claims.verbatim: only 34 of 340 approved Telecom Program requests in Alaska relied on Methods 1 or 2
claims.source_outlet: Alaska.Ai arithmetic on Federal Communications Commission figures
claims.notes: Derived claim, members named. 340 minus 34 equals 306. 306 divided by 340 equals 0.9000, exactly 90.0 percent. Licensed because both numbers count the same population. It licenses ONLY the statement that these requests did not rely on Methods 1 or 2. It does NOT license saying they used Method 3.

claims.claim: Subtracting the FCC's own figures, 285 of Alaska's 317 approved Telecom Program requests in funding year 2024 did not rely on Methods 1 or 2, which is about 89.9 percent.
claims.verbatim: only 32 of 317 approved Telecom Program requests relied on Methods 1 or 2
claims.source_outlet: Alaska.Ai arithmetic on Federal Communications Commission figures
claims.notes: Derived claim, members named. 317 minus 32 equals 285. 285 divided by 317 equals 0.8991. Corroborates C11 across a second year, so roughly nine in ten holds for both years and is not a one year artifact.

claims.claim: The FCC cites Alaska as its example of what it calls a significant decline in Telecom Program applications relying on Methods 1 and 2.
claims.verbatim: there has been a significant decline in the number of Telecom Program applications that have relied on Methods 1 and 2. For example, in Alaska,
claims.notes: Alaska is introduced by the words For example. The deck should not claim Alaska is the only state cited.

claims.claim: The FCC says its hierarchical approach to rural rates gives priority to Methods 1 and 2 and reflects a preference for commercial rates over the cost studies available under Method 3.
claims.verbatim: The hierarchical approach to determining rural rates, which assigns priority to Methods 1 and 2, represents a preference for the use of commercial rates over the use of cost studies available under Method 3.
claims.notes: The only wording in the notice that characterises the three Methods, and the safe basis for the deck's fallback framing. The notice does not formally define any of the three, so the deck must describe them in these terms and no further.

claims.claim: The FCC says the Rural Health Care Program consists of two component programs, the Telecommunications Program and the Healthcare Connect Fund Program.
claims.verbatim: The Rural Health Care (RHC) Program consists of two component programs: (1) the Telecommunications (Telecom) Program, and (2) the Healthcare Connect Fund (HCF) Program.
claims.notes: Telecom Program is a component of the Rural Health Care Program, which is in turn a Universal Service Fund program.

claims.claim: The FCC says the Telecom Program was established in 1997 and subsidizes the difference between rural and comparable urban rates for eligible telecommunications services used by health care providers.
claims.verbatim: The Telecom Program, established in 1997, subsidizes the difference between the rates for eligible telecommunications services in the health care provider's rural area and rates for comparable services available in urban areas within that state.
claims.notes: Explains why the rural rate determination Method matters. The Method sets the rural rate, and the rural rate sets the subsidy.

claims.claim: The FCC asks whether artificial intelligence tools used to review applications, audits and appeal review processes would help reduce delays while maintaining accurate results.
claims.value: 1 question on applications, audits and appeals
claims.verbatim: Would using artificial intelligence (AI) tools to review applications, audits, and appeal review processes help reduce delays while maintaining accurate results?
claims.notes: The central quote for the deck. Reproduced identically on three fetches. It is a question, not a proposal.

claims.claim: The FCC asks whether the fund administrator should expand its use of artificial intelligence in document review for audits and program compliance.
claims.verbatim: Should the administrator expand use of AI in its document review for audits and program compliance?
claims.notes: The word expand implies some AI use already exists at USAC. The notice does not say what that use is, so the deck must not characterise it.

claims.claim: The FCC asks whether there are operational inefficiencies that could be improved using artificial intelligence.
claims.verbatim: Are there operational inefficiencies that could be improved using artificial intelligence (AI)?
claims.notes: First AI mention in the document, in section A.1.

claims.claim: The FCC asks what the financial impact of incorporating artificial intelligence into the administration of the Universal Service Fund would be.
claims.verbatim: What would be the financial impact of incorporating AI into the administration of USF?

claims.claim: The FCC asks what safeguards would need to be put in place to ensure data integrity, governance and quality assurance if artificial intelligence is incorporated.
claims.verbatim: If AI is incorporated, what safeguards need to be put in place to ensure data integrity, governance, and quality assurance?
claims.notes: Shows the FCC is asking the safeguard question too, which keeps the deck's framing fair rather than one sided.

claims.claim: The FCC asks how privacy and information security concerns should be balanced against the potential benefits of using artificial intelligence in its universal service programs.
claims.verbatim: How should any privacy and information security concerns be balanced with potential benefits of using AI in relation to our USF programs?

claims.claim: Nine separate sentences in the FCC's universal service administration notice name artificial intelligence or AI.
claims.verbatim: Are there operational inefficiencies that could be improved using artificial intelligence (AI)? What processes could be improved with AI, if any? Should AI be used to reduce operational turnaround times and costs?
claims.source_outlet: Alaska.Ai count of Federal Communications Commission text
claims.notes: Derived count, members named. Seven sentences in section A.1, one in A.2 and one in A.3. A mechanical string count returned nine standalone occurrences, matching sentence by sentence.

claims.claim: One paragraph of the FCC's universal service administration notice poses eight consecutive questions about artificial intelligence.
claims.verbatim: Should AI be used to reduce operational turnaround times and costs? In what ways should it be used? Would efficiency in stakeholder engagement be improved with using AI resources to respond to stakeholder questions?
claims.source_outlet: Alaska.Ai count of Federal Communications Commission text
claims.notes: Derived count, members named. The full paragraph was returned verbatim twice and contains exactly eight question sentences, all about AI. This is the safer headline number than C23 because every one of the eight is unambiguously about AI.

claims.claim: Every mention of artificial intelligence in the FCC's universal service administration notice is phrased as a question, so the FCC is asking about AI rather than proposing it.
claims.verbatim: At the outset, we seek comment broadly on ways to strengthen the administration, management, and oversight of the Fund.
claims.notes: Load bearing for the deck's honesty. All nine AI sentences end in a question mark and none is phrased as we propose. The deck must never say the FCC proposed or planned to use AI.

claims.claim: The FCC did not name Alaska anywhere in the universal service administration notice that raises the artificial intelligence questions.
claims.verbatim: At the outset, we seek comment broadly on ways to strengthen the administration, management, and oversight of the Fund.
claims.notes: Absence claim, weaker by nature. Two independent full text extractions of the notice returned no occurrence of the word Alaska. The verbatim field carries the notice's own scope sentence, because a page can't quote a word it does not contain. Do not build a slide that depends on the absence being exhaustive.

claims.claim: The FCC did not write artificial intelligence or AI anywhere in the rural telehealth notice that names Alaska.
claims.verbatim: there has been a significant decline in the number of Telecom Program applications that have relied on Methods 1 and 2. For example, in Alaska,
claims.notes: Absence claim, same caveat as C26, confirmed by full text extraction. This is the fact that keeps the deck honest, because it means the link between the two notices is the deck's argument and not the FCC's. The verbatim field carries the Alaska sentence's own lead-in.

claims.claim: The FCC says the Universal Service Administrative Company administers the Universal Service Fund and that the Commission oversees those processes.
claims.verbatim: the processes used by Universal Service Administrative Company (USAC) to administer the USF and the Commission's oversight of those processes
claims.notes: Supports the deck saying USAC administers and the FCC decides. Taken from the notice's own summary section.

claims.claim: The FCC says the Universal Service Administrative Company's total operating expenses in 2025 were 266,603,608 dollars.
claims.verbatim: In 2025, USAC's total operation expenses were $266,603,608.
claims.notes: Returned on two fetches. The source's own wording is operation expenses, not operating expenses. Quote it as written if quoting.

claims.claim: The FCC says the Universal Service Administrative Company's operating expenses in 2025 were 3.06 percent of operating expenses plus disbursements.
claims.verbatim: In 2025, USAC's operating expenses were 3.06% of operating expenses plus disbursements.
claims.notes: The denominator is unusual and the deck must state it. It is expenses plus disbursements, not disbursements alone, so this is not a simple overhead rate.

claims.claim: The FCC seeks comment on reducing the size of the Universal Service Administrative Company Board from 20 members to 13 members.
claims.verbatim: Specifically, we seek comment on reducing the size of the USAC Board from 20 to 13 members.
claims.notes: Phrased as seek comment, not as an adopted change. The deck must say the FCC is asking, not cutting.

claims.claim: The FCC says that in 2025 its Bureau issued six orders affirming audit findings by the Universal Service Administrative Company which saved ratepayers over 9 million dollars.
claims.verbatim: For example, in 2025 the Bureau issued six orders affirming USAC audit findings, which saved ratepayers over $9 million.
claims.notes: The FCC's own characterisation of savings, one sided by nature, so attribute it in the deck. Relevant because audits are one of the processes the AI question in C17 names.

claims.claim: The FCC seeks comment on whether expanding the 30 percent speed restriction may promote expanded use of Method 1 or 2.
claims.verbatim: We seek comment on whether expanding the 30% speed restriction may promote expanded use of Method 1 or 2.
claims.notes: The sentence that immediately follows the Alaska numbers, so it shows what the FCC wants those Alaska numbers to inform.

claims.claim: The FCC says that in 2019 it defined similar services to include services with advertised speeds 30 percent above or below the speed of the requested service.
claims.verbatim: In 2019, the Commission defined "similar services" to include services with advertised speeds 30% above or below the speed of the requested service.
claims.notes: Explains what the 30 percent restriction in C33 actually is, so the deck can name it without hand waving.

claims.claim: Neither FCC notice gives Alaska or any other state a separate comment deadline or a separate filing route.
claims.verbatim: Pursuant to Sec. Sec. 1.415 and 1.419 of the Commission's rules, 47 CFR 1.415, 1.419, interested parties may file comments and reply comments on or before the dates indicated in the DATES section of this document.
claims.notes: Absence claim across both documents, checked in each. Both notices route all filers through the same rules and the same DATES section.

killed.claim: The FCC notice asks ten separate times whether artificial intelligence should be used to administer the fund.
killed.why: Wrong by one. A mechanical string count returned nine standalone occurrences spanning nine distinct sentences. The tenth sentence in the section A.1 run is In what ways should it be used?, which refers to AI only by the pronoun it. Replaced by C23 at nine sentences and C24 at eight consecutive questions.

killed.claim: Roughly nine in ten of Alaska's approved Telecom Program requests use the Method 3 fallback route.
killed.why: The document supports only that they did not rely on Methods 1 or 2. It never says the remainder used Method 3, and the sentence describing what must be justified under which Method came back inconsistently across two fetches. Use C11 instead.

killed.claim: Method 1 is the tariffed rate, Method 2 is the median of available rates and Method 3 is a cost study.
killed.why: Neither notice defines the three Methods, and no primary definition could be reached because ecfr.gov redirected to an unblock page and the govinfo CFR path for 47 CFR 54.604 returned 404. C14 is the only licensed characterisation.

killed.claim: The FCC proposes to use artificial intelligence to review Universal Service Fund applications, audits and appeals.
killed.why: The FCC asks, it does not propose. All nine AI sentences are interrogative and the notice's own summary says the Commission seeks comment. See C25. This distinction is the difference between a true deck and a false one.

killed.claim: Alaska's share of Rural Health Care Program funding is some stated percentage.
killed.why: No primary source was reached for any such figure. Killed rather than sourced to memory.

killed.claim: The two FCC notices are connected, or the FCC had Alaska in mind when it asked its AI questions.
killed.why: Unsupported and contradicted by C26 and C27. The AI notice never says Alaska and the Alaska notice never says AI. The link is the deck's argument and must be presented as the deck's argument.

killed.claim: The Universal Service Administrative Company already uses artificial intelligence in document review.
killed.why: Only inferable from the word expand in C18. The notice never states any current AI use, its scale or its nature. Too thin to assert.
